news.headline: Health ministry proposes amendment to drug rules to bring antimicrobials under regulatory oversight
news.story_lead: Health ministry proposes amendment to drug rules to bring antimicrobials under regulatory oversight New Delhi, Nov 19 (PTI) The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has proposed bringing antimicrobials under the Central regulatory framework applicable to new drugs to strengthen oversight of their quality, safety and efficacy and address antimicrobial resistance. It has proposed an amendment to the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019, through a draft gazette notification dated November 6, seeking to include antimicrobials in the definition of new drug under Rule 2(1)(w)(v). Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major global public health concern and a priority requiring coordinated action, the ministry said.
news.full_article_text: Health ministry proposes amendment to drug rules to bring antimicrobials under regulatory oversight New Delhi, Nov 19 (PTI) The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has proposed bringing antimicrobials under the Central regulatory framework applicable to new drugs to strengthen oversight of their quality, safety and efficacy and address antimicrobial resistance. It has proposed an amendment to the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019, through a draft gazette notification dated November 6, seeking to include antimicrobials in the definition of new drug under Rule 2(1)(w)(v). Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major global public health concern and a priority requiring coordinated action, the ministry said. The G20 New Delhi Leaders' Declaration also underscored the need to address antimicrobial resistance through a 'One Health' approach. "The proposed amendment has been initiated in view of concerns regarding the grant of manufacturing licences for antimicrobial products without adequate regulatory scrutiny, including the requirement for studies such as bioavailability/bioequivalence and stability studies," the ministry said. "The absence of such assessments may affect the quality, safety and efficacy of antimicrobial products. Substandard or ineffective antimicrobials can contribute to the development and spread of antimicrobial resistance, posing risks to patient safety," it added. The proposed amendment seeks to bring antimicrobials within the regulatory framework applicable to new drugs under the 2019 rules. Accordingly, manufacturers would be required to obtain permission from the Central Licensing Authority (CLA) before applying for a manufacturing licence from the concerned State Licensing Authority (SLA). This is expected to strengthen the Central regulatory oversight and help ensure the quality, safety and efficacy of antimicrobial products, the ministry said. The draft notification invites objections and suggestions from stakeholders and members of the public before the proposed amendment is considered for finalisation by the Centre. Antimicrobials are agents that kill microorganisms or stop their growth. They include medicines used to treat or prevent infections, as well as substances applied to skin or surfaces to reduce microbes. - Ministry Of Health And Family Welfare

news.full_article_text: Sub-panel formed to assess environmental, social impacts of Arunachal’s Kamala Hydroelectric Project The project proposal involves nearly 2.59 million trees in total, out of which 2.34 million are proposed to be felled The statutory body under the Union environment ministry that evaluates proposals to divert forest land has formed a three-member sub-committee to study the scale and potential implications of the 1720 MW Kamala Hydroelectric Project, which will involve diverting over 3,200 hectares of unclassified forest land and felling 2.34 million trees and bamboo in Arunachal Pradesh. The National Hydroelectric Power Corporation (NHPC) project will involve a concrete gravity dam at 216 metres from its deepest foundation and will eventually submerge around 2,665 hectares. The decision to review the project proposal was taken at a meeting of the Forest Advisory Committee (FAC), the statutory body, on October 23. The FAC noted the project involves “extensive submergence of forest land, affects a substantial number of trees, besides raising significant ecological and socio-economic concerns”. HT has seen the minutes of the FAC meeting. The project proposal involves nearly 2.59 million trees and bamboo in total, out of which 2.34 million are proposed to be felled. “This includes 1.508 million trees in the Hapoli forest division and 831,897 trees in the Kra Daadi forest division. No tree felling is proposed in the Kumey forest division,” the plan states. The FAC move coincided with protests against the proposed 11,200 MW Siang Upper project. Its sub-committee will include FAC members MM Pant and Nityanand Srivastava, and scientist Charan Jeet Singh. The minutes said the committee considered that the magnitude of the proposed diversion and its potential implications warrant a comprehensive assessment before the proposal is considered further. They added that a site visit will be required to assess the ecological implications of extensive submergence of forest land, including impacts on forest ecosystems, biodiversity, wildlife habitats and ecological connectivity. “They will have to examine the adequacy of the proposed mitigation measures, the component-wise requirement of forest land, and assess the feasibility of minimising the proposed diversion and submergence. It will also assess the extent of tree and bamboo loss arising from the proposed submergence and other project components, and examine the feasibility of avoiding or minimising such loss,” said the minutes. The FAC called for a focus on local communities. Around 1,300 families across six villages are likely to be affected by the project on the River Kamala, a major tributary of the Subansiri. The minutes noted that the user agency has mentioned that the Rehabilitation and Resettlement plan, once finalised by the District Administration, after complying with all statutory requirements, shall be furnished to the forest department for further needful action. Compensatory afforestation is proposed over 6,698 hectares of degraded forest land, not in Arunachal, but in Madhya Pradesh. “...it is more than twice the area of forest land proposed for diversion. Initially, out of 156 sites covering 7,043 ha, only 115 sites covering 5,248 ha were found suitable for afforestation. Gandhiok has over a decade of experience in journalism and is based in Delhi. He has reported extensively on Delhi and the National Capital Region (NCR). This includes the region's air pollution woes, a polluted Yamuna and on urban wildlife still thriving in the region. He joined HT in October 2021. Prior to that, he had five-year stint at The Times of India in Delhi, where he also covered Delhi, with a focus on environment and wildlife. Gandhiok has covered some recent events around the Capital too, ranging from the farmers' protests, the northeast Delhi riots and the CAA-NRC protests, reporting from the ground on all of these. He also travels across the country to report on how environment and climate change impact everyday life, while also writing on endangered species. His reports in 2019 on toxic leachate from Delhi's landfills led to the National Green Tribunal (NGT) taking suo motu cognisance and ultimately asking the state government to start bio-mining to flatten and remove all three landfills in the capital. Soni warned that ignoring transport workers, exploiting them and failing to address their demands could have serious political consequences for the government in the future. news.full_article_text: Road safety no licence for arbitrary highway demolitions: Supreme Court The apex court directed the affected property owners to approach their respective high courts to challenge the proposed demolitions. The Supreme Court has held that its April order directing the removal of unauthorised structures along national highways cannot serve as a blanket justification for demolitions, making it clear that the jurisdictional high courts must independently examine the legality of individual properties and their alleged encroachment on highway land. In an order on Wednesday, a bench of justices Vikram Nath and Aparesh Kumar Singh said the April 13 directions, issued in the larger interest of road safety, did not conclusively determine the rights of individuals or establish that particular structures constituted unauthorised encroachments. The order comes as relief to several property owners facing demolition. The court directed the affected property owners to approach their respective high courts to challenge the proposed demolitions, while ordering that existing interim protection would continue until the disposal of those proceedings. It further restrained the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) and other authorities from demolishing disputed structures or taking any coercive action pursuant to the impugned notices in cases where no such protection had earlier been granted. "We clarify that the directions dated April 13, 2026 shall not be treated as having conclusively determined the rights of the parties or the legality of the disputed structures," the bench said. The clarification comes after several property owners, particularly in Gujarat, approached the Supreme Court, apprehending the demolition of structures they claimed stood on privately owned land and had not been acquired or compensated for by the authorities. They disputed the demarcation of the right-of-way (ROW) undertaken by NHAI and questioned the legality of notices proposing the removal of their properties. The court acknowledged that while the removal of unauthorised encroachments from national highways was essential for public safety, the authorities could not presume that every structure they identified as an encroachment was necessarily unauthorised. "The distinction between a general direction to remove encroachments and the determination of whether a particular property constitutes an encroachment is of considerable significance. The former cannot, by itself, be treated as a conclusive adjudication of the latter," it said. The April 13 order directed highway authorities to identify and remove unauthorised structures within the right-of-way of national highways, including dhabas, eateries and other commercial establishments. It also mandated that district administrations constitute highway safety task forces and enforce the removal of existing and new unauthorised structures within 60 days, in accordance with the Control of National Highways (Land and Traffic) Act, 2002. However, the bench underlined that these directions did not authorise authorities to bypass the statutory procedure governing removal of alleged encroachments under the 2002 law. It said the provision contemplated the issuance of a notice identifying the highway land in question, an opportunity for the affected person to make a representation, and consideration of the explanation before coercive action could be taken. While the law did provide for removal without prior notice in specified circumstances under subsections (7) and (8) of Section 26, the bench said the availability of such powers had to be examined against the statutory conditions governing their exercise. The April directions, it added, could not independently justify dispensing with the requirements of the law. "A mere assertion of ownership or lawful occupation cannot, by itself, prevent the authorities from exercising their statutory powers to remove unauthorised encroachments. Equally, the mere assertion by the authorities that a particular structure falls within the Right of Way cannot be treated as a substitute for the determination required under law, where the very basis of such assertion is disputed," it said. The applicants had relied on registered sale deeds, revenue records, acquisition documents and permissions granted by competent authorities to contest the proposed demolitions. Some also alleged that the measurements and demarcation carried out by NHAI were incorrect, while seeking acquisition and compensation wherever their land was required for highway widening or other public purposes. NHAI, on its part, maintained that the action was being undertaken in compliance with the Supreme Court'sCourt'sdirections and that notices had been issued under the 2002 Act. It also contended that the measurements established that the disputed structures fell within the right-of-way, and that disputes over ownership and boundaries involved factual questions requiring adjudication by the competent forum. The bench said such disputes would be better examined by the jurisdictional high courts, which could scrutinise revenue records, acquisition proceedings, survey reports and other relevant material, and determine whether the authorities had followed the procedure prescribed by law. It made clear that it had expressed no opinion on the merits of the property owners' claims or on the correctness of the action initiated by NHAI. All questions concerning ownership, demarcation of the right-of-way, acquisition of land, and statutory compliance would remain open for independent consideration. The interim protection, however, was strictly confined to the structures that were the subject matter of the applications and would neither create any equity in favour of the applicants nor authorise any fresh construction or encroachment. The court said its April 13 directions would otherwise continue to operate in their entirety, preserving the larger road-safety exercise while ensuring that action against alleged encroachments remained subject to the law. - ABOUT THE AUTHOR Utkarsh Anand Utkarsh Anand is the National Legal Editor at Hindustan Times, where he leads the newspaper's coverage of the Supreme Court, constitutional law, the judiciary and the Union law ministry. Narendra Modi thanked Prince William for bringing his Earthshot prize to the country during the couple's first international tour since 2022. It comes a day after the royal couple gave out Â£1m prizes to winners of the environmental award , which was founded by the prince and remains one of his biggest personal projects. Catherine also visited a maternity hospital, where she comforted a grieving mother who lost a baby after giving birth to premature twin girls. - Street cricket with a legend then metro ride as William and Kate begin India visit Published 2 days ago On Wednesday, William and Catherine travelled from Mumbai to capital New Delhi for the final leg of their trip. The prince and princess also spoke "warmly" of their time in the country, thanking the prime minister and the people for their welcome, and saying how much they enjoyed returning to India, a decade after their last visit. news.headline: Israeli military launches rare ground operation in Gaza beyond Yellow Line
news.story_lead: Residents fled the area near Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camps following the Israeli evacuation order - Published 34 minutes ago Israeli ground forces have launched a rare operation in part of the central Gaza Strip outside their control, after issuing evacuation orders for residents. Witnesses said tanks advanced east of Nuseirat refugee camp and rolled onto the territory's main north to south road under the cover of artillery strikes. The Israeli military said the "targeted" operation aimed to dismantle a "terror tunnel" west of the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the more than 60% of Gaza's territory occupied by Israel.
news.full_article_text: Residents fled the area near Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camps following the Israeli evacuation order - Published 34 minutes ago Israeli ground forces have launched a rare operation in part of the central Gaza Strip outside their control, after issuing evacuation orders for residents. Witnesses said tanks advanced east of Nuseirat refugee camp and rolled onto the territory's main north to south road under the cover of artillery strikes. The Israeli military said the "targeted" operation aimed to dismantle a "terror tunnel" west of the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the more than 60% of Gaza's territory occupied by Israel. The Palestinian armed group Hamas, which controls the rest of Gaza, accused Israel of a "flagrant violation" of the October 2025 ceasefire agreement. Violence has continued in Gaza over the past 13 months, with near-daily Israeli strikes, and living conditions for the 2.1 million people there remain dire. Early on Wednesday afternoon, Israeli military body Cogat's Arabic spokesperson announced the start of the incursion and warned Palestinians living in an area north of Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camp to stay away for their own safety. It also said a section of the north to south Salah al-Din road that passed through the area would be closed to traffic. Later, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it had begun a joint operation with the Shin Bet security service "to dismantle a terror tunnel west of the Yellow Line that posed an immediate and direct threat to IDF troops". "IDF troops under the Southern Command are deployed in the area in accordance with the ceasefire agreement and will continue to operate to remove any immediate threat and thwart attempts by the Hamas terrorist organisation to harm Israeli civilians or IDF troops, or to violate the agreement," it added. Hamas warned in a statement that the advance of Israeli military vehicles beyond the Yellow Line and the evacuation of residents constituted "a dangerous development and a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement". Footage published by Palestinian media outlets and on social media showed families fleeing areas near Nuseirat camp following the announcement. In one video verified by BBC Verify, a man can be seen ducking after hearing artillery fire and then running along Salah al-Din road, about 1.5km (0.9 miles) west of the Yellow Line. "The Israeli occupation now is firing randomly near the houses and tents of people," he says. Automatic gunfire can be heard in another video filmed just to the south-east. A resident of Nuseirat who was forced to flee told BBC Arabic's Middle East Daily programme: "The situation is now extremely dire, with Israeli forces firing indiscriminately at areas where displaced people have sought shelter." "We couldn't take any of our belongings with us - not even our blankets, pillows, or clothes. We had no choice but to leave everything behind." A second resident also reported "indiscriminate gunfire and shelling" and said there had been "numerous casualties, including fatalities". Asked about reported fatalities, the IDF sent a general statement about the operation. - Israel building new land barriers in Gaza and displacing families Published 30 July - Israel moves Yellow Line deeper into Gaza, satellite images show Published 16 January Gaza's Hamas-run Civil Defence agency said three people were killed and others were wounded in three separate Israeli drone strikes on Wednesday. One man was killed in Nuseirat, the second to the north in Gaza City, and the third in the central town of Deir al-Balah, it added. The Israeli military said the first two strikes targeted "terrorists" and that it was not aware of the third incident, according to AFP news agency. At least 1,658 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the ceasefire began last year, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. The Israeli military says six of its soldiers have been killed over the same period. Meanwhile, more than 1.9 million people - about 90% of Gaza's population - remain displaced, with 1.4 million of them living in tents or makeshift shelters, according to the UN. Reconstruction has yet to begin in Gaza, where an estimated 82% of all structures have been destroyed or damaged during the war, as US President Donald Trump's peace plan has largely stalled. The disarmament of Hamas has been a key sticking point. The group has agreed to give up its weapons in exchange for a phased withdrawal of Israeli troops from the 60% of Gaza they currently occupy. But Israel has insisted that Hamas must fully disarm before any pullout. The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage. Since then, more than 74,700 people have been killed in Gaza, the health ministry says. news.full_article_text: PM sets target for drug abuse eradication at council of ministers meeting Modi urged a concerted campaign against drug abuse, while highlighting poverty reduction and gains against left-wing extremism. Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Wednesday chaired a meeting of the council of ministers and underscored the need for a concerted campaign to eradicate drug use, said people aware of the details. According to a person privy to the meeting, the PM expressed concern over the widespread social evil and said drug addiction had emerged as a major challenge for the country. He said just as the government took stern measures against left-wing terrorism and managed to pull out millions from poverty, there was a need to act against drug abuse, this person added. “The prime minister was overcome with emotions when he spoke about the impact drugs use has on the younger demographic and said the social evil needs to be eradicated and no effort must be spared to do so...” said the person quoted above. The Union government has sharpened its campaign against drug abuse, particularly in poll-bound Punjab. In recent weeks, anti-drug campaigns have been the focus of Bharatiya Janata Party leaders including Union home minister Amit Shah, who announced that the party would fight the upcoming assembly elections in the northern state on the plank of “Nasha Mukt Punjab”(drug-free Punjab). On November 9, Shah at an event in Gujarat said that the Modi government now aims at creating a ‘Drug-free India’ by December 31, 2029. At the three-hour meeting held at Bharat Mandapam in the Capital, two presentations on poverty alleviation and LWE eradication and cyber security were also made. The poverty alleviation presentation was made by Anuradha Thakur, secretary, Department of Economic Affairs (DEA) and LWE eradication was discussed by Govind Mohan, Union home secretary. “The presentation on poverty alleviation measures highlighted how 500 million people have been pulled out of poverty and the economic progress made over the past 12 years,” said the person quoted above. The PM is learnt to have said that when the government was formed in 2014, he had referred to it as the government for the poor. He urged his colleagues to ensure that poverty alleviation measures were implemented well so that more people could have a quality life with access to health and education. Regarding the government’s achievements in curbing left-wing extremism, the PM cautioned that the government and law enforcement agencies must maintain their vigil to ensure that Maoism did not make a comeback. “The government set itself a target to eradicate Naxalism and has been successful in doing so. The PM said both achievements, of alleviating poverty and curbing LWE, need to be celebrated,” said the person quoted above. The ministers also discussed a World Bank poverty report stating that 500 million people were lifted out of poverty between 2011 and 2023, reducing the extreme poverty rate by 90%—from more than one in four Indians to roughly one in 38. The discussions also centered on governance reforms, employment generation, 100% saturation of welfare schemes, and targeted outreach toward youth and women—demographics heavily tied to India’s innovation and entrepreneurship push. - ABOUT THE AUTHOR Smriti Kak Ramachandran Smriti covers an intersection of politics and governance. news.full_article_text: Supreme Court seeks Centre’s response on delay in finalising judges’ appointment procedure SC sought response of Centre, Secretary General of top court on petition seeking finalisation of amended MoP for appointment of judges to constitutional courts The Supreme Court on Wednesday sought the response of the Centre and the Secretary General of the top court on a petition seeking finalisation of an amended Memorandum of Procedure (MoP) for appointment of judges to the constitutional courts. The MoP is a set of documents governing the appointment, elevation and transfer of high court and Supreme Court judges. A bench of Justices MM Sundresh and PB Varale issued notice on a petition filed by Lok Prahari, an NGO, which questioned the delay in finalising the MoP despite a clear direction by a Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court in 2015 while striking down the National Judicial Appointments Commission and reviving the Collegium system for appointing judges to the Supreme Court and High Courts. Following the judgment which sought improved functioning of the Collegium system, an order was passed on December 16, 2025 for the Centre to finalise the existing MoP by supplementing it with the decisions taken by Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant based on the unanimous view of the Collegium of the four senior-most judges of the top court. The petition also sought to bring the minutes of the selection process conducted by the Collegium of the Supreme Court and High Courts under the Right to Information (RTI) Act. The petition stated that since the issue relates to the appointment of judges, the matter deserves urgency because the dispensation of justice depends on the quality of judges appointed. The petition filed by advocate Shashank Singh said, “...the existing MoP suffers from the serious flaws of lack of transparency and objectivity affecting the quality, and thereby, the performance of the judges of the constitutional courts, directly affecting the litigants’ right to justice promised in the Preamble to the Constitution.” The petition named the Union of India and the CJI through the secretary general as respondents since the 2015 order required the CJI to take a decision on the MoP based on the unanimous view of the Collegium. “Ten years’ time was more than enough to comply with the decision of the Constitution Bench,” the petition said, adding, “Evidently, its implementation has been unduly delayed for no valid reason and it is a case of persistent breach of duty on the part of the respondent no. 1 (Centre) to comply with the order in this matter of great national and public importance relating to the top judiciary of the country.” The petition urged the court to issue a direction for finalising the MoP within a month and to ensure transparency and objectivity in the selection process by allowing the minutes of the meetings of the High Court and Supreme Court Collegiums for the selection of judges to be accessible to the public under the RTI Act.
